Abstract
Smart agriculture and smart breeding are evolving from isolated sensing toward geographically distributed, long-term, data-driven closed-loop management. Dispersed farms and breeding sites, UAV and remote-sensing phenotyping, real-time field control, edge inference, and digital-twin synchronization impose heterogeneous demands on coverage, latency, bandwidth, reliability, computing, and energy. Space–air–ground integrated networks (SAGINs) combine satellites, unmanned aerial vehicles/high-altitude platforms, and terrestrial networks for wide-area coverage and elastic access, but introduce dynamic topologies, heterogeneous multi-domain resources, and complex cross-layer orchestration. Focusing on intelligent SAGIN resource management enabled by software-defined networking (SDN) and network function virtualization (NFV), this review examines controller placement, NFV/service function chain orchestration, SDN/NFV cooperation, learning-driven optimization, and security mechanisms. Representative studies are compared by objectives, decision variables, mechanisms, applicability boundaries, and engineering costs. These mechanisms are connected to smart agriculture and smart breeding through ubiquitous connectivity, edge computing, task offloading, phenotyping, and digital-twin closed loops, while distinguishing experimentally supported agricultural evidence from SAGIN-oriented architectural inference. 11. Conclusions
Motivated by the digital-infrastructure requirements of smart agriculture and smart breeding, this review systematically examines progress in SDN- and NFV-enabled SAGIN resource management. Across SDN controller placement, NFV/SFC orchestration, SDN/NFV cooperation, learning-driven resource management, and security mechanisms, primary evidence is compared in terms of optimization objectives, decision variables, solution mechanisms, application scenarios, quantitative gains, and engineering costs. Smart agriculture and smart breeding are used to test the practical requirements of cross-domain resource management for connectivity, computing, task offloading, phenotypic sensing, and digital twins. The literature shows a clear transition from static, single-domain, single-objective optimization toward closed-loop management that combines dynamic cross-domain state sensing, service orchestration, and learning-based decisions. For agricultural applications, the value of this transition lies in organizing remote coverage, mobile sensing, edge processing, and long-term model synchronization within one schedulable infrastructure rather than simply adding another communication link. Explicit trade-offs nevertheless remain between controller count and control latency, SFC benefit and migration cost, learning performance and communication/computing overhead, and security gain and service acceptance.
